intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · tectonics to contours

Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

intro_cards.title: Worked contour gradient
body: Two points: 1 200 m and 1 000 m. Map distance between them is 4 cm. Scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m).
Rise = 200 m. Run = 4 × 500 = 2 000 m. Gradient = 200/2000 = 1 in 10 (or 10%). Write both the fraction and a sentence: “For every 10 m walked horizontally you climb 1 m.”

units.title: Human Settlement
units.intro:
A **settlement** is a place people occupy with some permanence — a seasonal camp, a village, a town, a city. Geography asks *where* and *why there*, then *what the place does*.

**Site** is the exact piece of ground: a spring, a dry point above a marsh, a hill for defence, a bridging point, a sheltered harbour, a mining outcrop. Site answers “why this plot?”

cards.title: 4.1 What is Settlement?
body: **A settlement** is a place where people come to build their houses and live.
**Settlements** are the expressions of human occupancy of the earth’s surface.
Settlements are purposefully organized clusters of houses and non-residential buildings.
Settlements reflect the relationship of human beings with their environment.
Settlements also reflect the social, economic, and cultural aspects of society.

cards.title: Settlement: fuller notes
body: A **settlement** is a place where people live. **Site** is the actual land it is built on (water supply, defence, flat land, building materials); **situation** is its position in relation to the surrounding area (roads, rivers, other towns, resources). Settlement patterns: **nucleated** (houses grouped together), **dispersed** (houses scattered, as on large farms) and **linear** (houses along a road, river or coast).

cards.title: Worked example: site factors
cards.problem: Give three site factors that might explain why an early village grew near a hilltop spring.

steps.text: **Water supply**: the spring provides water all year.
**Defence**: the hilltop gives a good view of approaching danger.

cards.answer: **Dry, firm land**: above flood level and good for building.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The form of settlement created when houses are built along a river side, is known as
cards.why: **Linear settlements** are characterized by buildings arranged in a line. This pattern typically develops along transport routes like roads, or natural features like **river banks** and coastlines, where access to the resource or transport is prioritized.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Settlements that developed on a site where houses **spread out in several directions** along major roads will be:
cards.why:
A **star-shaped** settlement pattern develops when buildings are constructed along several roads that radiate out from a central point or intersection. 
- **Linear:** Along a single road/river.
- **Grid:** Planned with streets at right angles.
- **Radial:** Similar to star but often more circular around a center.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A type of settlement build by farmers like the sheepherders at a distant place is:
cards.why: Isolated or dispersed settlements consist of single houses or farms scattered over a wide area, common in pastoral or farming regions where people live far from each other.

cards.title: Rural Settlements
body: **Situation** is the place in the wider network: on a highland–port road, in the middle of a farming basin, at a border. Situation answers “why this plot stayed important when weapons or wetlands changed.” A good harbour (site) that sits on a world shipping lane (situation) becomes a city; a good harbour at the end of nowhere may stay a village.

**Functions** change through time. A place may start as a market, add administration, then industry or a port. Most real towns are multi-functional; the exam still wants you to name the *dominant* one and a piece of evidence (docks, ministries, factories, shrine).

**Rural settlements** in Eritrea include highland farming villages and lowland pastoral / agro-pastoral camps. Pattern may be nucleated (clustered around water or a church/mosque) or dispersed (farmsteads in fields).

cards.title: 4.2.1 Basic factors that determine the site of rural settlements
body: The needs for space by human beings are of primary importance for human settlements.
A place that presents these requirements provides an ideal site for settlement.
The environment provides the site, building materials, and other resources like water that may influence the location of settlements in general.
Factors that influence the location or site of rural settlements are directly related to the livelihood systems of rural people.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Types and patterns of rural settlements
body: Rural settlements vary in type, distribution, pattern, size, shape, and other characteristics due to various physical and cultural (human) factors.
The distribution and pattern of rural settlements can be approached in two ways.
Rural settlements can be classified into three types on the basis of size.
Isolated buildings emerge when farmers build their shelter on their farms at a distance from the nearest village or hamlet.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Classification of rural settlements
body: One classification is on the basis of permanence of the settlement.
Ephemeral, if they last 1-7 days in a particular place. b.
Temporary, if they last 1-30 days in a place. c.
Seasonal, if they last several months in a place. d.

cards.title: 4.2.4 Function of rural settlements
body: Settlements are created to satisfy economic, social, political technological and cultural needs of people.
Over time they may assume additional functions.
Settlements develop through a continuous process and require continuous investment.
The importance of every settlement largely depends on its location or position within the whole system of settlements.

cards.title: 4.2.5 Evolution of rural settlements
body: Up to about 13, 000 B.C.E., people depended on hunting and gathering for their living.
After this, which was also the end of the Ice Age, changing environmental and demographic conditions caused major changes in the hunter-gatherer societies.
Technological improvements led to sedentary settlements in areas that had abundant and seasonally predictable food resources.
Domestication of plants and animals started in various parts of the world.

cards.title: 4.2.6 Place names
body: Settlements, whether urban or rural, are identified by names.
The study of the origins and meaning of place names is called **toponymy**.
**Place names** are the product of ecological diversity, cultural perception, and wealth of places.
Place names are helpful in establishing relationships between different regions or even within the same region.

steps.text: Situation links inland and overseas trade.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On the basis of permanence, if rural settlements last 1 – 30 days in a place, they are called ________ settlements.
cards.why: Settlements are classified by their duration. Ephemeral settlements are very short-term, lasting only a few days to a month (1-30 days), often used by nomadic herders or for very brief resource gathering.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Rural settlements classified into isolated building, hamlet and village. This classification system is on the bases of
cards.why: The classification into isolated buildings (single houses), hamlets (small clusters), and villages (larger clusters) is based on the **size** and population of the settlement.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: ________is a type of rural settlement if people last several years in a particular place.
cards.why: **Permanent settlements** are those where people live for a long period, often many years or generations, as opposed to nomadic or seasonal movements.

cards.title: Urban Settlements
body: **Urban growth:** trade, colonial administration, industry, and rural–urban migration. In many developing countries the built-up area and informal housing race ahead of piped water, jobs and formal titles. In richer cities the story is often suburban sprawl plus later attempts to revive the old centre.

cards.title: Revision checklist (say these out loud)
body:
- Wadi = same jobs, seasonal burst.
- Site = the plot. Situation = the network.

cards.title: 4.3.1 The Nature of urban settlements
body: Cities are among the oldest marks of civilization.
Since their first appearance 4000 to 6000 years ago, they have continued to emerge and grow or die.
Cities are part of a larger, urban and rural society and economy.
Cities show an orderly internal arrangement of land uses, social groups, and economic functions.

cards.title: 4.3.2 Factors of town location
body: For a town to perform its functions, it must be located at a suitable position.
Centrality, good transport facility, resource availability, flat terrain, and other factores encourage the growth of urban settlements.
**Site** refers to the actual physical quality of the place a town or city occupies.
Terrain features of the place on which a city is located and its absolute location are the two basic site features.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Functions of towns
body: Towns, irrespective of their size, age or location, exist to perform certain functions that cannot be carried out in dispersed locations.
Usually, towns that have a larger number of different kinds of functions grow very fast and become large in size.
Manufacturing: These are towns mainly engaged in the manufacturing of goods.
Pittsburgh, Detroit and Michigan in the USA and Tokyo in Japan are manufacturing cities.

cards.title: 4.3.4 Emergence and growth of urban settlements
body: The emergence of sedentary agriculture led to fixed settlements, but for many years, settlements remained truly rural.
The emergence of specialised segments of society (farmers, artisans, soldiers, merchants, elites, and others) gave to the need for new political systems.
Groups of settlements came under one central authority.

Later this process spread to other places like the Nile delta, Indus valley, Mediterranean Europe, Mesoamerica, and other places The emergence of central authority and the need to administer territories from a single location gave rise to the emergence of towns.

cards.title: 4.3.5 Cities in developing countries
body: With increasing population, the area occupied by towns and cities increases.
As cities expand, thousands of hectares of agricultural land is used for non-agricultural purposes thereby decreasing food production.
The growth of housing in many towns of the less developed countries is much slower than their population growth.
Many cities like Nairobi, Jakarta, Mexico City and Cairo are surrounded by densely populated slums and shantytowns.

cards.title: 4.3.6 Cities in developed dountries
body: One of the major problems faced by such cities is traffic congestion.
Beijing has over three million cars, and driving in such towns is extremely difficult and time consuming.
Traffic congestion is particularly high during rush hours when the roads are crowded with taxis, private cars and buses.
The presence of too many cars and industries means too much pollution.

cards.title: Explain the growth of a town from its site and situation
cards.problem: Explain why Massawa grew into an important town, using the ideas of site and situation.

steps.text: **Step 1: Define the terms.** Site = the physical ground the town stands on; situation = its position in relation to surrounding areas and routes.
**Step 2: Site.** Massawa stands on islands and a sheltered natural harbour on the Red Sea coast, with deep water for ships.
**Step 3: Situation.** It lies on the Red Sea shipping lane and is linked by road and railway to Asmara and the highlands, so goods enter and leave the country through it.
**Step 4: Functions.** These advantages gave it port, trade, fishing and administrative functions, which attracted people and services.
**Conclusion:** a good harbour site plus a central trading situation made Massawa a major port town.

cards.answer: Its sheltered deep-water harbour (site) and its position on the Red Sea route linked to the highlands (situation) gave it port and trade functions that drew people and services.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A term used to indicate the merging of several cities to create a single mega city is
cards.why: A megalopolis (or conurbation) is formed when several large cities and their surrounding metropolitan areas grow and merge into one continuous urban region.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The process of merging or coalescence of urban settlements is called ______________.
cards.why: A **conurbation** is a region comprising a number of cities, large towns, and other urban areas that, through population growth and physical expansion, have merged to form one continuous urban or industrially developed area.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which factor most directly explains why many towns grow up at river crossings or road junctions?

options.D: Good accessibility for trade and transport

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A town needs people and goods to reach it easily.

**Step 2:** Bridging points and junctions are places where routes meet, so trade and services concentrate there.

**Step 3:** Cold climate, steep slopes and lack of water discourage town growth.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

tips.text: Settlements emerged and developed over a long period of time.

A settlement refers to a place where people have come to build their houses and live. They show the manner in which human beings establish themselves on the earth’s surface, and they reflect people’s relationship with their environment.
By studying the site, pattern, and arrangement of settlements, we can understand something about how people used their surroundings.
Settlements are broadly divided into rural and urban.
The distinction between urban and rural is based on occupation rather than size.

In urban settlements, the major occupation of people is trade or industry while in rural areas most of the people live by farming. However, there is no universally accepted definition of urban settlements.
Thus each country uses its own definition or classification.
The majority of the population of developing countries live in rural settlements, while the majority of population of developed countries live in urban settlements.
However, the rate of urbanization is higher in the less developed countries than in developed countries at present.
Many rural dwellers are moving to towns and cities in the less developed countries due to rural push and urban pull.

cards.front: Tap: site vs situation of Massawa
cards.back: Site: hot coastal strip, natural harbour, islands that shelter shipping. Situation: the Red Sea door into the Eritrean highlands — road and historic rail to Asmara — and a place on the Suez–Indian Ocean sea lane. The heat is a site problem; the trade role is situation.

cards.front: Tap: site vs situation of Asmara
cards.back: Site: highland plateau, milder climate, room to build. Situation: command of the route down the escarpment to Massawa and of roads across the plateau — capital and service centre for the densely settled highlands.
The place in the wider network: on a highland–port road, in the middle of a farming basin, at a border.

questions.q: Rural settlements are **distinguished** from urban settlements by:
why: The primary geographical distinction between rural and urban areas is the **economic activity**. Rural areas are dominated by **primary activities** (agriculture, fishing, mining), while urban areas focus on **secondary and tertiary activities** (industry, services).
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The type of settlement that last 1 to 7 days in a place is
why: Settlements are classified based on their duration. **Ephemeral settlements** are very short-lived, typically lasting only a few days (1-7 days), often associated with nomadic groups or specific short-term activities.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The type of settlement formed, when farmers built their houses in their farm lands is:
why: When farmers build houses far apart from each other, each on its own piece of farmland, it forms an **isolated** or **dispersed** settlement pattern.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: A settlement that consists of about a dozen of houses is a
why: A hamlet is a very small human settlement, typically smaller than a village and often consisting of only a few (about a dozen) houses.

questions.q: The kraals of sub-Saharan Africa are good examples of __________________ settlements.
why: A **kraal** is a traditional African village or enclosure for livestock, typically built in a **circular or rounded** shape for protection and social organization.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Houses spread out in several directions along major roads. This form of settlement is
why: A **radial settlement** pattern occurs when buildings are arranged along several roads leading out from a central point, such as a market or crossroads.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: One of the following statements is wrong statement about human settlement?
